sections.text: You can pay off a mortgage years early with extra monthly payments, bi-weekly payments or lump sums, and all three work. What decides how much they save is less the method than the start date. On a $350,000 loan at 6.75%, adding $300 a month from day one saves $151,699 in interest and ends the loan 8 years 5 months early. The same $300 started after year 5 saves $99,222.
Why early payments are worth the most

Mortgage interest is charged on the outstanding balance, so it is heaviest at the start. On a 30-year, $350,000 loan at 6.75%, the monthly principal-and-interest payment is $2,270.09. The first payment carries $1,968.75 of interest, which is 86.7% of it, and only $301.34 reduces the balance. Across year one, interest is $23,511 and principal is $3,730. Every dollar you prepay in those years stops accruing interest for the rest of the loan, which is why timing dominates.

Assumptions: $350,000, 30-year fixed at 6.75%, payment $2,270.09, no prepayment penalty, extra money applied to principal each month. Baseline interest over the full term is $467,234. Years below are counted from the first payment.

headers: Start paying an extra $300 a month

sections.text: Waiting five years costs $52,477 of the potential savings, even though the monthly sacrifice is identical. Late starters still benefit, but the savings fall quickly because less interest remains to be avoided.
The same idea for a one-time lump sum
The three strategies on this loan

items: Extra monthly payment: $300 more every month, started on day one, totals about $77,700 of extra payments and saves $151,699 in interest.

Bi-weekly payments: half the payment every 14 days, 26 times a year, equals 13 monthly payments. Modeled with interest accruing at one twenty-sixth of the annual rate per payment (6.75% / 26) and payments credited on arrival, it ends the loan in about 23 years 11 months and saves $111,478. Real servicers differ, so this is a best case, and it only works if your servicer actually credits each half payment when received.
Lump sums: a one-time $10,000 at closing saves $59,262 and ends the loan 2 years 6 months early. A lump sum from a bonus or refund helps most when paid as early as possible.
Skipping the principal-only instruction. Ask your servicer how to designate extra money as principal, and confirm it on the next statement.

Prepaying before the safety net exists. A paid-down mortgage is hard to turn back into cash. Keep an emergency fund, clear higher-rate debts first, and take any employer retirement match before sending extra to the mortgage.

Assuming the interest saved is certain profit. It is a guaranteed saving at your loan rate, but money invested elsewhere may earn more or less. Returns are uncertain and past performance does not guarantee future results, so this is a trade-off to weigh, not a rule.
Forgetting other costs. Taxes, insurance and any mortgage insurance are separate from principal and interest and do not shrink because you prepaid.

sections.text: The table assumes a fixed rate that never changes. With an adjustable-rate loan, a rate reset changes the maths. Loans with prepayment penalties can wipe out the benefit, so read your note first. If you plan to sell in a few years, you only avoid the interest that would have accrued until the sale, so most of the savings shown here never materialise; the money simply comes back as equity at closing.
Every number on this page came from a month-by-month simulation using the mortgage payoff calculator's logic. Enter your own balance, rate and payment to see your exact payoff month.
